questions.explanation: A clause requiring others to assist on request, decided collectively, is an automatic commitment rather than a statement of intent. Nothing in the note limits it to frontier fighting.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the Berlin blockade became a crisis
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a currency decision turned into an international crisis
questions.stem: Marked on the projection, a zone around a divided city is dated from one year to the next, and the sheet asks for an account of how a currency decision turned into a crisis.

answer.exemplar: The crisis began as an administrative dispute about money. The western authorities in a divided city issued a new currency, declaring it the sole legal tender in their zones, in order to end the inflation of the old currency and to separate the western economy from the eastern one. The Soviet authorities regarded the introduction as an act of currency separation from the rest of their own zone, and reacted by sealing the land and water routes into the city. A city of roughly two million people was suddenly cut off from the surrounding country, and what had been an economic manoeuvre became a test of who controlled the city and of whether the postwar settlement could be enforced. The blockade also exposed a weakness: the western powers had assumed that the agreements dividing Germany would hold as long as the western zones were politically separate from the eastern one.

questions.explanation: The sheet asks how a currency decision became a crisis, so the answer must trace the new currency, the Soviet reaction and the sealing of the routes. The last point shows the settlement's assumptions were tested.
questions.hint: Trace the chain from the new note to the sealed routes.

questions.topic: Why an airlift answered the blockade
questions.learningObjective: Explain why an airlift was chosen to answer a blockade

options.text: Because sending aircraft avoided both a military confrontation and any concession on the currency dispute.
Because the aircraft could carry far more tonnage per day than any convoy of trucks.
options.misconception: compares capacity without checking the constraint

options.text: Because the western zones had no ports or railways left after the blockade cut them off.
options.misconception: invents the destruction of the port and rail links

options.text: Because the corridor routes had been prepared years earlier for exactly this kind of emergency.
options.misconception: claims advance preparation the summary does not record

questions.explanation: The choice was made because troops risked war and withdrawal conceded the currency issue. Aircraft supplied what the sealed routes no longer could, and the tonnage shows the scale reached.
questions.hint: Think about the two things the response had to avoid.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The end of the occupation of Japan
questions.learningObjective: Explain the terms by which an occupation of Japan was ended
questions.stem: In the projection room, a sheet dates the end of the military occupation and a legend marks the bases that remained.

answer.exemplar: The occupation ended because a settlement was reached that both sides could accept, and the terms show what was and was not settled. A treaty restored the sovereignty of the state and gave the new constitution, which the state had adopted and which renounced war as an instrument, a formal standing. A separate security agreement kept foreign forces in the country under a treaty arrangement, so the end of the occupation did not mean the end of the foreign military presence. Reconstruction and rearmament then proceeded under the restored government, which was given the right to establish a modest defence force. The result was a state that was independent in law and limited in practice, a settlement that satisfied the need for order without recreating the conditions that had led to the earlier war.

questions.explanation: The sheet asks for the terms of the ending, so the answer must distinguish the treaty restoring sovereignty from the agreement keeping foreign bases. Treating the end of occupation as full withdrawal misses the point.
questions.hint: Sort the agreements by what each one settled.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The automatic defense commitment in western Europe
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the consultation clause of a mutual defence article

stimulus.body: A treaty article of 1949 states that if an armed attack is made against one of the parties, each of the others will assist the party attacked with such military and other assistance as it deems necessary, including the use of armed force. It adds that any such assistance will be the subject of consultation among the parties.

questions.stem: The cartographer's note beside a hatched area asks what the article's consultation clause means in practice.

options.text: It means that each party may decide alone whether to intervene, since consultation is only informative.
options.misconception: reads consultation as leaving the decision entirely free

options.text: It means that the article creates an automatic declaration of war on the attacking party.
options.misconception: confuses collective assistance with an automatic declaration of war

options.text: It means that an attack triggers an obligation to assist, even though the form of that assistance is coordinated.
It means that the article has no effect unless every single party agrees to the form of assistance in advance.
options.misconception: requires unanimity the article does not demand

questions.explanation: The obligation to assist is stated unconditionally, while consultation governs how assistance is arranged rather than whether it is given. That is what makes it automatic in substance and coordinated in form.
questions.hint: Ask what consultation governs and what it does not.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The first Soviet nuclear test
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose and consequences of a first nuclear test
questions.stem: Sketched in a cartographer's notebook, a note asks for an account of why the Soviet Union tested a nuclear device in the summer of 1949 and what followed from it.

answer.exemplar: The test was carried out in a remote area of Soviet central Asia, at a site chosen for its distance from populated regions and for the secrecy the terrain allowed. The device was of an original design and the method of its construction differed in important respects from the design used in the American bomb, so that even if the arrangement were observed from the air it would not be copied directly. The immediate effect was to end the period in which only one power possessed such a weapon, and to remove the assumption on which American defence plans rested. In the United States the effect was immediate and severe: the decision to build a hydrogen bomb was taken soon afterwards, the small existing stockpile was greatly expanded, and the idea that a monopoly could be maintained indefinitely was abandoned. The test also confirmed what intelligence had already suggested, that the Soviet programme was further advanced than the west had believed, and that the gap between the two arsenals would be measured in years rather than in a generation.

questions.explanation: The note asks for reasons and consequences, so the answer must cover the strategic purpose of a test and the effect of ending the monopoly. It should close on the arms race it helped begin.
questions.hint: Cover the site, the device and the reaction.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The decision to cross the dividing line in 1950
questions.learningObjective: Explain how an intervention was authorised when one council was blocked
questions.stem: Pinned under a sheet, a memorandum asks for an account of how a decision to cross a dividing line was taken in the presence of a walkout from the Security Council.

answer.exemplar: The sequence of the decision explains a good deal about why it was taken as it was. The council was unable to act because one of the permanent members had withdrawn its representative and refused to take part in any discussion, so a resolution condemning the crossing could not be carried. Two other members, having concluded that the movement could not be stopped, asked for the authorisation of the assembly instead, and the assembly voted by a clear majority to call for the withdrawal of the attacking forces and for members to provide assistance. The security council was then asked to approve the use of force under that authorisation, and the request was approved with the absent member not participating. Command arrangements were settled in the same period, with the forces that would assist given the specific task of defending the southern part of the peninsula and the line that divided it. The result was an international operation under the assembly's authority, and one that the permanent member whose absence had blocked the council could not have prevented, though it chose to stay away from it.

questions.explanation: The memorandum asks how the decision was made, so the answer must trace the blocked council, the assembly, the authorisation and the command arrangements. The last point shows why the procedure mattered.
questions.hint: Trace the institutional route from complaint to authorisation.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the Berlin blockade became a crisis
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a crisis over one city was settled without a war
questions.stem: Along the frontier drawn in red, a note asks for an account of how a crisis over one city was settled without a war between the occupying powers.

answer.exemplar: The crisis was settled by a combination of measures that none of the parties had prepared for. The airlift kept the western zones supplied, which removed the immediate military necessity that the blockade had created. Because the western powers did not withdraw the new currency, the status quo before the crisis was not restored either, and the currency of the eastern zone circulated only in the east. Negotiations then produced an arrangement under which the two currencies would be traded for one another at a fixed rate, so that the western zones could obtain eastern currency for purchases without the eastern authorities accepting the western note as legal tender in their own territory. The city itself remained divided, and a wider agreement on the future of Germany was deferred rather than settled. The result was that the immediate confrontation was defused and both sides avoided the costs of trying to reverse it by force, at the price of accepting a division that was now hardened and institutionally managed rather than temporary.

questions.explanation: The note asks how the crisis was settled without war, so the answer must combine the supply measure, the refusal to restore the previous currency and the negotiated exchange. The last point shows what was postponed.
questions.hint: List the measures that defused the confrontation.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The automatic defense commitment in western Europe
questions.learningObjective: Explain why western European states sought a collective guarantee
questions.stem: Annotated on the sheet, a paragraph asks for an account of why western European states in the late 1940s sought a guarantee from each other.

answer.exemplar: The guarantee answered a set of specific fears that had been sharpened by the previous decade. Governments had seen what happened when a state was left to rely on distant promises, and several of them had recently signed agreements that left them dependent on a great power across an ocean. Others had been occupied and were reluctant to place their security again in the hands of a power that had withdrawn from them before. There was also the memory of states that had been defended in the 1930s by arrangements which had collapsed when the first test came, and the fear that an American withdrawal or an American commitment that proved conditional would leave smaller states unprotected. A collective guarantee among European states themselves answered all of this at once: it made aid to the attacked automatic, it gave the smaller members a voice in decisions about their own defence, and it reduced the sense that each was standing alone in a dangerous neighbourhood.

questions.explanation: The note asks for reasons behind a guarantee, so the answer must draw on the occupation, the unreliability of distant promises and the earlier decade's failures. Naming what the guarantee promised completes the account.
questions.hint: List the fears the guarantee answered.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The split inside the eastern bloc
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a break between the leading power and one member developed
questions.stem: Half drawn on tracing paper, a note asks for an account of how a break between the leading power and one of its own members came about.

answer.exemplar: The break grew out of a dispute over control. The leading power treated the socialist federation in its own sphere as a part of its own state system, and expected the party there to follow instructions as an organ of the bloc. The federation's leadership, having built a state on its own authority, its own security services and its own economic plans, expected the relationship to work as a partnership between equals. Between those two expectations there was no agreed rule to settle differences, so every disagreement became a test of the hierarchy. The public charges multiplied, each side accusing the other of betrayal, and the federation's exclusion from the bloc's organisation turned a quarrel into a formal breach. What followed showed how far the disagreement had gone: the federation built its own economic arrangements and its own defence posture, and the leading power answered by demanding the removal of those in the federation who were sympathetic to Moscow. The rivalry between the two then lasted for decades, and the bloc that had seemed to speak with one voice was split in two.

questions.explanation: The note asks how the break came about, so the answer must show two incompatible expectations clashing and the absence of any rule for settling them. The later consequences show why it became permanent.
questions.hint: Identify the two conflicting expectations.

questions.stem: A corridor shown on the map has a note listing the years each member joined and the obligations each accepted on joining.

options.text: The note shows that later members accepted the same clause as the founders, so the guarantee widened rather than changed.
The note shows that later members accepted weaker terms, so the guarantee weakened as it expanded.
options.misconception: invents a weakening of the terms

options.text: The note shows that the founding members retained a veto over the admission of any later member.
options.misconception: invents a veto the note does not record

options.text: The note shows that membership was limited to five states and could not be extended at all.
options.misconception: contradicts the note's list of joining years

questions.explanation: A single clause accepted unchanged by each new member shows a guarantee that extended without altering its terms. The note lists accessions and obligations, not conditions or vetoes.
questions.hint: Compare the obligations of first and later members.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the Berlin blockade became a crisis
questions.learningObjective: Read a transport bulletin as evidence of a centrally run operation

stimulus.body: A bulletin issued by the transport authority of the western zones records that a designated corridor would be kept open for scheduled flights between the western airfield and the city. It states that fuel would be supplied at fixed intervals and that the authority would publish daily figures of the tonnage carried.

questions.stem: In the projection notes, a bulletin asks what the arrangement shows about how the response was managed.

options.text: It shows that the operation was run as a matter of military necessity without any civil administration.
options.misconception: ignores the administrative detail in the bulletin

options.text: It shows that the corridors were left unmonitored so that neither side could object to them.
options.misconception: invents an absence of monitoring

options.text: It shows the operation was routine and centralised, with rules, supplies and published figures.
It shows that the authorities accepted full responsibility for the political dispute that had begun the crisis.
options.misconception: inflates a transport arrangement into a political settlement

questions.explanation: Fixed corridors, scheduled fuel and daily figures describe a routine operation run under fixed rules. That regularity is what made the response politically acceptable to governments that could not use troops.
questions.hint: Look at the administrative details the bulletin lists.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The decision to cross the dividing line in 1950
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a decision to intervene was taken and what it aimed at
questions.stem: The projection shows a chain of islands and a note asks for an account of how the decision to intervene was taken and what it was intended to accomplish.

answer.exemplar: The intervention was decided in three stages and each stage shaped the next. A military assessment concluded that the force which had crossed the line could not be contained by the local forces available and would continue to advance unless it was met, which removed the option of doing nothing. The political problem was that the body empowered to authorise the use of force could not function, because a permanent member had withdrawn its representative and refused to take part in any discussion of the complaint. A second permanent member therefore put the question to the general assembly, which approved a resolution calling on the attacking forces to withdraw and on members to provide assistance. On the strength of that authorisation the request to use armed force in the defence of the southern part of the peninsula was approved as well, with the absent member not participating in the vote. The intended result was limited: to halt the advance and restore the earlier line, which is why the commanders were given a restricted task and why the authority of the assembly was used throughout rather than any claim of acting on the council's behalf.

questions.explanation: The note asks for the decision and its purpose, so the answer must cover the military assessment, the assembly route and the limited objective set for the commanders. The closing point explains the war's shape.
questions.hint: Cover the assessment, the authorisation and the objective.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the Korean war ended where it began
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the arrangement reached was called a pause rather than a settlement
questions.stem: A line on the sheet marks the truce and a note asks why the arrangement reached was described as a pause rather than a settlement.

options.text: Because the agreement fixed military positions while leaving the political claims of both sides unresolved.
Because the agreement was reached quickly, leaving no time for the terms to be considered carefully.
options.misconception: explains the outcome by the speed of negotiation

options.text: Because the supervising body was given a long mandate, so the truce was expected to last for years.
options.misconception: misreads the supervision mandate as the reason for the pause

options.text: Because the agreement excluded the two governments from the negotiations that produced it.
options.misconception: invents an exclusion of the governments

questions.explanation: Fixing positions while leaving rival claims open is what makes an arrangement a pause. A settlement would have settled the status of the peninsula, and no agreement did that.
questions.hint: Ask what the agreement did and did not settle.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The first Soviet nuclear test
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the site and the announcement together carried a message
questions.stem: Drawn over a sketch of the test site, two annotations record the choice of location and the wording of the announcement that followed.

options.text: The annotations show that the location was chosen for its weather and the announcement was made to claim credit.
options.misconception: invents a credit-claiming announcement

options.text: The annotations show that the location was chosen for its secrecy and the announcement was made to warn of war.
options.misconception: misreads the announcement as a threat of war

options.text: The annotations show that the location was chosen for its resources and the announcement was made to invite talks.
options.misconception: invents an invitation to negotiations

options.text: The annotations show that the location protected the design and the announcement announced a capability.

questions.explanation: A remote site kept observers from learning the design, and a public statement announced a capability rather than a threat or an invitation. Together they describe a message about what others might assume.
questions.hint: Ask what each annotation contributed.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why an airlift answered the blockade
questions.learningObjective: Identify the feature that shows the airlift substituted for the closed routes
questions.stem: The cartographer's remark on a corridor diagram asks which feature of the airlift most clearly reveals that it was a substitute for the closed ground routes.

options.text: That the flights operated from airfields on the western side of the city itself.
options.misconception: misplaces the airfields inside the city

options.text: That every cargo had to be flown to the city's airfield and then carried inland by other means.
That the routes were surveyed by engineers of the eastern authorities at the war's end.
options.misconception: invents eastern survey work

options.text: That the operation was funded by contributions collected from the eastern zones themselves.
options.misconception: invents an eastern funding arrangement

questions.explanation: Flying to the edge of the city and relying on other means for the last part shows the operation was designed to replace the ground routes. A complete air delivery would have needed no such stage.
questions.hint: Think about what happened to cargo after landing.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The automatic defense commitment in western Europe
questions.learningObjective: Read a circular as evidence of how a guarantee was meant to operate

stimulus.body: A foreign ministry circular of 1949 instructs representatives to inform their governments that the guarantee of assistance applies to an armed attack against any of the parties. It directs that requests for assistance should be conveyed to the standing committee of the organisation without delay.

questions.stem: A grid square on the chart asks what the circular shows about how the guarantee was meant to operate.

options.text: It shows that the guarantee depended on each representative judging for himself whether an attack had occurred.
options.misconception: invents a national assessment stage

options.text: It shows that the request for assistance had to be approved by the standing committee before it could be made.
options.misconception: reverses the order of request and approval

options.text: It shows that the guarantee applied to attacks on any state whatsoever, wherever it occurred.
options.misconception: widens the guarantee beyond the parties

options.text: It shows that the guarantee covered any armed attack on a member and that the request went straight to the committee.

questions.explanation: The circular states a guarantee against armed attack on a member, with a request conveyed directly and without delay, so no national filter weighed it first. A general application would be a different arrangement.
questions.hint: Read the two instructions together.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The split inside the eastern bloc
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a dated list as evidence of a member's exceptional position
questions.stem: The sheet's title block records the years in which each member of the bloc admitted new parties to its own leadership or permitted them to operate.

options.text: The list shows that every member admitted new parties at the same time in each year of the period.
options.misconception: claims a synchronised pattern the list does not show

options.text: The list shows that the members with the largest armies permitted new parties earliest.
options.misconception: invents a military explanation

options.text: The list shows that new parties were admitted only in the years immediately following the split.
options.misconception: asserts a link to the split the list does not fix

options.text: The list shows that permitting new parties was an exception in one member while the others did not.

questions.explanation: One member permitting new parties while the others did not is the pattern a rupture inside a supposed uniformity would produce. The list records timing, and does not explain the differences.
questions.hint: Compare the rows rather than reading them separately.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The end of the occupation of Japan
questions.learningObjective: Explain what limited rearmament reveals about the new order
questions.stem: In the atlas's front matter, a note asks what the rearmament permitted during the years after the occupation ended reveals about the settlement.

options.text: It reveals that the state was intended to become the dominant military power in its region.
options.misconception: inflates limited rearmament into regional primacy

options.text: It reveals that the new order allowed a state to exist but not to become a threat to its neighbours.
It reveals that the state's armed forces were placed under a foreign commander.
options.misconception: invents a foreign command of the forces

options.text: It reveals that rearmament was postponed indefinitely because of opposition from the occupying power.
options.misconception: contradicts the note's own timeline

questions.explanation: Limited rearmament permitted while sovereignty returned shows a settlement for independence without restoring the capacity that had made the earlier war dangerous. The forces allowed were small.
questions.hint: Compare the scale of the forces permitted with the war's scale.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The automatic defense commitment in western Europe
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the guarantee reached beyond national borders
questions.stem: On the surveyor's chart of western Europe, a shaded band links the members and the note asks why the arrangement was drawn across national borders rather than kept within them.

options.text: Because the borders themselves were considered the main danger that had to be overcome.
options.misconception: treats borders as the threat rather than the setting

options.text: Because the members had decided to merge their armies into a single integrated command.
options.misconception: invents an integrated command not mentioned

options.text: Because the threats they faced lay outside their own frontiers, so the response had to reach across them.
Because the organisation's secretariat insisted that its membership cover whole continents.
options.misconception: invents a geographical rule imposed by officials

questions.explanation: A guarantee that reaches outside national frontiers is aimed at threats from outside them. Keeping the arrangement within borders would have left the actual danger uncovered.
questions.hint: Ask where the danger the members faced came from.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the Berlin blockade became a crisis
questions.learningObjective: Explain the double character of the response to the blockade
questions.stem: The sheet's title block names a blockade and an airlift in the same year, and the note asks what the pair shows about how the crisis was handled.

options.text: They show that pressure was answered with supply rather than force, and the division hardened rather than being undone.
They show that the blockade failed completely, because the city continued to trade with the surrounding country.
options.misconception: overstates the effect of the blockade

options.text: They show that the airlift was intended to break the blockade by attacking the aircraft that enforced it.
options.misconception: invents an offensive purpose for the airlift

options.text: They show that both measures ended within a few weeks, so the crisis was shorter than it appeared.
options.misconception: contradicts the length of the operation

questions.explanation: Answering a blockade with aircraft rather than troops kept the dispute out of a war, but left the currency and the division as they stood. A method that avoided war while leaving the quarrel untouched has that double character.
questions.hint: Ask what was avoided and what was left standing.
